title: VPNs
subtitle: A VPN is one of the most misunderstood tools in privacy. It's useful for some things, irrelevant for others, and marketed as solving problems it doesn't really touch. This guide covers whether you need one, what to consider when picking a provider, how to use one safely, and a comparison of four popular providers.

context.title: What does a VPN even do?
context.body: A VPN encrypts the connection between your device and the VPN provider's server, then sends your traffic out to the internet from there. Two things follow from that: your internet provider can no longer see what sites you're visiting (only that you're connected to a VPN), and the sites you visit see the VPN's IP address instead of your own. That's the entire mechanism, so everything a VPN can or can't do for you follows from those two facts.
context.body2: It does not make you anonymous, it does not stop a website from tracking you once you're logged in, and it does not protect you from malware, phishing, or a weak password.

warning.body: Always assume your online activity is being tracked, monitored, and stored to some degree. If you're looking to browse the internet anonymously, refer to more in-depth technical guides like The Hitchhiker's Guide to Anonymity, which you can find linked on our Resources page.

sections.label: Do you really need a VPN?

items.name: Use cases for VPNs
items.why: A VPN is useful for specific scenarios and might not be useful for everyone. If none of these apply to you, it may not be worth the cost or the mild performance hit.

steps.text: `You use public wifi often` → a VPN prevents others on that same network from snooping on your web traffic
`Privacy from ISPs` → you want to stop your internet provider from seeing which sites you visit
`Government censorship` → you travel to or live somewhere with government censorship and need to reach blocked content
`Apparent location` → you want your apparent location to be somewhere other than where you actually are
You do not need a VPN just to "be more private" in general - most day-to-day privacy problems (account tracking, data broker profiles, weak passwords) are better addressed by other actions

items.name: What VPNs cannot do
items.why: VPN marketing frequently implies a level of protection that the technology doesn't provide. Understanding a VPN's limits prevents a false sense of security.

steps.text: `Tracking` → a VPN can't stop a website from tracking you across the web once you've logged into an account. You're still you, VPN or not. Your account will now just be associated with that IP address
`Phishing, malware, weak passwords` → a VPN doesn't protect against phishing, malware, or a weak or reused password
`Browser fingerprinting` → a VPN won't make your browser fingerprint disappear. Sites can still identify your device through screen size, fonts, installed extensions, and other signals
`Anonymity` → a VPN does not make you anonymous

sections.label: What to look for in a provider

items.name: Independently audited no-logs policies
items.path: Check on the provider's transparency / audit page
items.why: Any company can write a privacy policy that says "we don't log anything." Look for VPNs that have had an independent third party verify their claims, and whether the policy has held up under legal or physical pressure. For example, a police raid, court case, or server seizure.

steps.text: Look for audits from a named, reputable security firm, published in full
Prefer providers with more than one audit, since a single audit is not an ongoing guarantee
Weigh real-world tests (a seizure, a subpoena, a court case) more heavily than a paid audit. These are the closest thing to proof that a no-logs policy works under pressure

items.name: Consider the provider's legal jurisdiction
items.path: Check where the company is legally headquartered
items.why: A provider based in a country with strong privacy laws and are outside of the Five Eyes / Nine Eyes / Fourteen Eyes intelligence-sharing alliances are going to be a safer bet for your data. Jurisdiction matters a bit less if the provider has no logs to hand over.

steps.text: Switzerland and Sweden are commonly cited as privacy-favorable jurisdictions outside the major surveillance alliances
The US, UK, Canada, and Australia are all Five Eyes members, which some may want to take into consideration

items.name: Look for anonymous payment and signup options
items.path: Check the provider's payment methods page
items.why: A no-logs policy protects your traffic, but your payment method can still tie your identity to your account. Providers that accept cash by mail or cryptocurrency, or that only require a username and password rather than an email or ID, reduce that link.

steps.text: Check whether the provider accepts cash, cryptocurrency, or gift cards in addition to standard payment methods
If you pay by card or a personal email tied to your name, the account can be tied back to you, regardless of the VPN provider

items.name: Confirm the app has a working kill switch
items.why: A kill switch blocks all internet traffic if the VPN connection drops unexpectedly, preventing your IP address and unencrypted traffic from leaking out while the app reconnects. Without one, a momentary disconnection from the VPN service will expose your IP address.

steps.text: After installing, check the app's settings for a kill switch or "block traffic if VPN disconnects" option and enable it
Test it by disabling your wifi briefly while connected, and confirm no traffic gets through until the VPN reconnects

items.name: Keep the VPN connected by default
items.path: App settings → Auto-connect / Connect on startup
items.why: A VPN only protects the traffic that passes through it while it's active. Leaving it off most of the time and turning it on only when you remember to defeats the purpose.

steps.text: Enable auto-connect or connect-on-startup in the app's settings so it's on by default
Turn it off only for specific sites that block VPN traffic, then reconnect immediately after

items.name: Avoid unknown free VPN apps
items.path: Applies especially to app store search results
items.why: Running a VPN service costs money for server infrastructure. A free VPN from a provider with no clear business model is very often monetizing your traffic directly. Either through ad injection, data resale, or in some documented cases, selling access to your device's bandwidth as a residential proxy for someone else's traffic. Look into the Onavo VPN and how it was used by Facebook to spy on users.

steps.text: Only use a free tier from a well-known and trusted provider
Be especially cautious of free VPN apps found only in an app store search, with no public company behind them and no audit history

items.name: When Tor is a better fit than a VPN
items.why: A VPN moves trust from your internet provider to the VPN provider. You're still putting your trust in a third-party service provider that more or less knows who you are. Tor routes your traffic through independent volunteer relays, so no single party sees both who you are and what you're doing. For anonymity needs, that's a better option than a VPN.

steps.text: For everyday privacy while on the internet, a good VPN is the right tool

For situations where you specifically cannot afford any single party to link your identity to your activity, use the Tor browser instead of a VPN. See the Hitchhiker's Guide to Anonymity for detailed instructions on how to make yourself anonymous online
It's generally not recommended to use a VPN while using the Tor browser unless you're an advanced user, as you can accidentally compromise your identity even while using Tor

sources.label: The Hitchhiker's Guide to Online Anonymity

items.name: A VPN is for network privacy, not digital anonymity
items.why: This is the most common misunderstanding about VPNs. They do not provide anonymity. A VPN hides your traffic from ISPs and hides your IP address from the websites you visit. It does nothing to stop those websites from identifying you through logins, cookies, browser fingerprinting, or the account you're signed into.

steps.text: If you log into an account, email, social media, a shopping site, that site knows exactly who you are, VPN or not
Browser fingerprinting (screen size, fonts, timezone, installed extensions) can re-identify you across sessions even while logged out and connected to a VPN
The VPN provider can still see your IP address and likely much of your activity (even if that activity is not stored or is anonymized to some degree)
